item.title: A Grayscale-Compatible Color Encoding via 8-bit HSV Bit-Packing and Lightweight Refinement
item.description:
The problem

Converting a colour image to grayscale makes it compact and keeps it compatible with grayscale pipelines, but it throws away all chrominance. Colourization networks try to bring the colour back from the gray image alone. They are typically large, and because the input carries no explicit colour anchor, the colours they produce come from learned priors and can be wrong for the scene.

Invertible-grayscale methods instead hide colour inside an 8-bit gray-like image, either by modifying pixel values (reversible data hiding) or with learned invertible networks. The image they produce looks like a grayscale picture but is not guaranteed to be bit-identical to the standard grayscale, and the neural variants usually require heavier encoder–decoder networks. This paper takes a different design point: a 16-bit single-channel carrier whose high byte is the standard BT.601 grayscale, with the second byte spent on an explicit colour hint. It is intentionally not a replacement for strict 8-bit storage: it uses 16 instead of 8 bits per pixel, still down from 24 for RGB.

How it works

The encoder is a fixed bit-packing rule with no learned parameters. The decoder first rebuilds a coarse colour image deterministically from the packed bits, then a small U-Net refines it.

  1. Gray in the high byte. For each pixel, the standard ITU-R BT.601 grayscale value (0.299 R + 0.587 G + 0.114 B, rounded to 8 bits) is stored in the 8 most significant bits of a 16-bit word.
  2. Quantize hue and saturation. The pixel’s hue (OpenCV range 0–179) and saturation (0–255) are each quantized to 4 bits. This balanced split, H4S4, was chosen by the bit-allocation ablation.
  3. Pack the low byte. The 4-bit hue and 4-bit saturation are packed into the low byte (8 bits in all), the HSV hint. Shifting the word right by 8 bits returns the standard grayscale exactly: gray PSNR is infinite and gray SSIM is 1.0.
  4. Direct decoder. Without any training, the word is unpacked, hue and saturation are dequantized, the gray value is used as V, and HSV is converted back to RGB. This gives a coarse colour image.
  5. Residual refinement. The main model (UNet-residual) is a two-level U-Net with 0.47 M parameters. It takes the coarse RGB together with the gray, hue and saturation planes (6 channels) and adds a residual scaled by 0.25; the result is clipped to the valid range. Two direct-prediction variants of the same size serve as ablations: UNet-gray sees only the gray plane, and UNet-hints sees gray, hue and saturation (3 channels).

Results

Grayscale plane bit-identical to BT.601: gray PSNR = ∞ and SSIM = 1.0 by construction (Section II-E, Table XI).
Kodak 24 PSNR from 23.89 dB to 40.64 dB, and CIEDE2000 ΔE00 from 10.40 to 1.63, as the explicit chroma hint given to the U-Net grows from 0 bits (UNet-gray) to 8 bits per pixel (UNet-hints) (Table VIII).
0.47 M parameters, 14.77 GFLOPs, 1474 FPS at 256 × 256 for UNet-hints (the residual variant runs at 757 FPS), against two invertible-grayscale baselines with an 8-bit carrier: WIN 2025 at 2.34 M / 76.75 GFLOPs / 68 FPS and Zhao 2021 at 14.63 M / 129.05 GFLOPs / 18 FPS (Table VI). WIN 2025 reaches higher PSNR than UNet-hints on Kodak 24.

All networks are trained on the 5,000-image PASCAL VOC 2012 subset (80/20 train/val) and tested at 256 × 256 on Kodak 24, the DIV2K validation set (100 images) and McMaster 18. The low-byte hint carries most of the colour: the U-Net that sees gray, hue and saturation (UNet-hints) reaches 40.64 dB on Kodak 24, 38.10 dB on DIV2K and 35.41 dB on McMaster, while the same network given only the gray plane reaches 23.89, 22.98 and 18.61 dB. The direct decoder alone, with no network, gives 26.05 dB on Kodak 24. The residual variant reaches 37.88, 37.60 and 31.26 dB; the authors attribute its gap on the saturated McMaster images to the residual scale of 0.25, which limits how far it can correct a weak direct reconstruction. Among the re-measured baselines, WIN 2025 scores higher on most metrics (40.96 dB on Kodak 24, 38.16 dB on DIV2K and 39.43 dB on McMaster). The authors stress that these comparisons are not rate-normalized, since the baselines use an 8-bit carrier and this method a 16-bit one.

The format is fragile under lossy processing of the 16-bit image. JPEG at quality 90 lowers Kodak PSNR of the residual pipeline from 37.88 dB to 22.02 dB, and a Gaussian blur of σ = 0.5 to 16.32 dB, because both mix or discard the bits of the hint byte. If the hint byte is dropped entirely, the output falls back to a near-grayscale image (22.79 dB, SSIM 0.931). The authors therefore recommend the format for pipelines that keep the 16-bit image lossless, for example 16-bit PNG.

item.title: A Reversible Grayscale Method Based on Bit-Field Multi-Channel Fusion Encoding
item.description:
The problem

Grayscale images are widely used because they cut computational complexity, storage and transmission cost. In many applications, though, the original colours are needed again later, so the conversion should be reversible: the grayscale image has to carry enough colour information to restore the RGB image.

Traditional reversible grayscale methods, such as histogram shifting and wavelet-packet data hiding, embed colour cues into the luminance channel. They usually impose extra transform-domain constraints or need several auxiliary channels, which adds computation and memory. Deep-learning methods reach high reconstruction fidelity but bring high inference latency, large models, limited interpretability and a strong dependence on training data.

How it works

The method needs no training. Each RGB pixel is converted to the HSV colour space, which separates the chromatic part (hue H, saturation S) from the luminance part (value V). The three components are quantized to a, b and c bits with a + b + c = 16 and written side by side into the bit fields (H in the high bits, V in the low bits) of one 16-bit grayscale pixel. Decoding reads the fields back with shifts and masks. The whole pipeline uses only quantization and bitwise operations, and it is exactly invertible except for the quantization error.

  1. Normalize. The three channels of an 8-bit RGB pixel are divided by 255, so they lie in [0, 1].
  2. RGB to HSV. The standard conversion gives hue H as an angle from 0° to 360°, saturation S and value V; H is then scaled to [0, 1).
  3. Allocate the 16 bits. The output pixel’s 16 bits are split into a bits for H, b for S and c for V. The split can follow the image statistics, with a and b proportional to the variances of H and S and c taking the rest. The paper also gives four example schemes; the balanced Scheme 1 uses (6, 4, 6).
  4. Quantize and pack. H, S and V pass through a non-linear (gamma) mapping that favours perceptually sensitive ranges, are quantized to 2a, 2b and 2c levels, and are packed as IG = (Hq ≪ (b + c)) | (Sq ≪ c) | Vq. The result is a single-channel 16-bit grayscale image.
  5. Decode. Bit masks and shifts recover Hq, Sq and Vq; inverse quantization and the standard HSV-to-RGB transform give the 8-bit RGB pixel back.

The choice of (a, b, c) trades accuracy between the channels. Because people are sensitive to hue changes, the authors recommend a ≥ 5 (32 hue levels) to avoid visible colour shifts, and c ≥ 6 (64 value levels) to prevent banding; b can be reduced for images with little colour. Hue is circular, so a non-linear quantization keeps errors small near 0°/360°, and Floyd–Steinberg error diffusion spreads the remaining quantization error spatially.

Results

Encoding 3.71 ms and decoding 7.01 ms per Kodak image with Scheme 1, against 175.30 / 125.24 ms for IDN and 2486.75 / 2453.82 ms for the CNN-based method (Table II).
PSNR 34.80 dB, SSIM 0.9726 on Kodak with Scheme 1; higher is better, and PSNR is below IDN (42.16 dB) and the CNN-based method (37.40 dB) (Table II).
PSNR 34.06 / 34.48 / 32.20 dB on Urban100 / BSD500 / McMaster with Scheme 1, with encoding and decoding times between 2.80 and 3.82 ms (Table III).

The method was evaluated on four datasets: Kodak PhotoCD (24 images), Urban100 (100 urban scenes), BSD500 (500 natural landscapes) and McMaster (18 images). It was compared with two learning-based invertible grayscale methods, IDN and a CNN-based method, using MAE, PSNR, SSIM, FSIM and LPIPS, and timed on an AMD Ryzen 9 7945HX with an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 4060. Of the four bit-allocation schemes, Scheme 1 (6, 4, 6) gives the best balance; Scheme 2 (5, 5, 6) reaches the highest SSIM of the four on Kodak (0.9779), and Scheme 4 (6, 5, 5) is the fastest at 3.21 ms encoding and 4.49 ms decoding. The 16-bit files are also slightly smaller on Kodak: 633.20 KB for Scheme 1, against 721.47 KB for IDN and 660.87 KB for the CNN-based method (Table II).

The speed comes at a cost in fidelity. On Kodak, IDN reaches 42.16 dB PSNR and the CNN-based method 37.40 dB, against 34.80 dB here, and the authors note that a recent reversible data-hiding method reports 43.69 dB. They see the method as a lightweight, interpretable alternative for resource-constrained settings such as edge and embedded systems, and plan adaptive allocation algorithms and reversible compression to close the quality gap, and FPGA/ASIC implementations to further cut latency.

item.title: Parallel Grayscale Connected Component Analysis via Neighborhood Labeling and Global Region Mapping
item.description:
The problem

Connected component analysis (CCA) groups adjacent pixels with similar values into regions. It is a basic step in industrial defect detection, depth-map filtering and medical tissue identification. As sensors reach higher resolutions, industrial lines need it on megapixel images within milliseconds, without losing segmentation fidelity.

The existing options trade one for the other. Serial CPU algorithms such as region growing and flood fill work directly on grayscale intensity and keep fine structure and subtle gradients, but are too slow for high-throughput production lines. Fast GPU algorithms, such as OpenCV’s connectedComponents, are designed for binary images. They need a binarization step first, for example Otsu thresholding, which discards intensity information. Low-contrast defects, or adjacent depth planes with similar intensities, are then merged or lost.

Adapting the binary GPU algorithms to grayscale is not straightforward, according to the authors. Binary images mostly consist of sparse, distinct blobs, whereas grayscale images have dense, continuous gradients. Linking neighbours whose intensities differ by at most a threshold creates far more temporary equivalences between pixels. In label propagation and parallel union-find this leads to heavy atomic contention on global memory, which destroys the parallel speed-up.

How it works

The method runs entirely on the GPU and works on the raw grayscale or depth values. Two neighbouring pixels belong together if their intensities differ by at most a threshold τ. Instead of merging pixel by pixel, it first cuts the image into small local regions, finds where those regions touch, and then merges them in the much smaller space of region IDs.

  1. Local partitioning. Each pixel looks at four neighbours already passed in raster order: upper-left, up, upper-right and left. It attaches to the first one, in that fixed priority order, whose intensity differs by at most τ; if none qualifies, it becomes a root. All pixels decide in parallel. Pointer jumping (path compression) then gives every pixel the ID of its root. Because the mask only looks backwards, some shapes, such as U-shapes, are split into several preliminary regions.
  2. Boundary detection. To find where those regions should join, each pixel checks its three neighbours below: lower-left, down and lower-right. If a neighbour has a different label but an intensity within τ, the pair of region IDs is written to an edge list with one atomic index increment. The edges form a region adjacency graph, which is much smaller than the image.
  3. Global region mapping. A mapping table over region IDs starts as the identity. For each edge, the larger ID is mapped to the smaller one; chains are followed to their current roots, so a region connected to several others ends up in one component. A final flattening pass makes every entry point straight to its root, and one pass over the image replaces each pixel’s label by its root.
  4. Feature aggregation. Region statistics such as the area are counted in each GPU block’s shared memory, in a small hash table, and then added to global memory once per block. This cuts the number of global atomic operations from one per pixel to roughly one per region and block, and the integer sums are exact and deterministic. Components below a minimum area can be filtered out in the same pass.

Results

1.567 ms on a 1920 × 1080 depth image, against 155.79 ms for serial region growing and 156.60 ms for flood fill (Image 1 of Table 4), about 1.32 gigapixels per second.
Grayscale detail is kept: on the same image, the binarize-then-label OpenCV pipeline finds 27 components, region growing 2,543 and the proposed method 2,586 (Table 4). With region growing as the reference, the average IoU over 8 depth maps is 99.98%.
Runtime barely depends on scene complexity: across 8 images of the same size it stays between 1.567 and 1.704 ms, while region growing ranges from 152.55 to 284.79 ms (Table 4).

The algorithm is implemented in CUDA C++ and was tested on an NVIDIA GeForce RTX 3060 with an Intel Core i5-12500 CPU; times are averages of 100 runs and exclude data transfer. The test images are industrial depth maps and grayscale images from 400 × 300 to 4000 × 3000 pixels. The baselines are OpenCV connectedComponents on the GPU, which needs a binary image, and serial region growing and flood fill on the CPU, which work on grayscale like the proposed method.

According to the authors, the binary pipeline over-merges or misses subtle grayscale components after thresholding, while the proposed method gives finer region partitions. OpenCV is still much faster, since it labels a binary image: 0.194 ms against 0.865 ms at 1920 × 1080 (Table 2). Against the grayscale baselines the gap is large at every resolution: at 4000 × 3000 the proposed method needs 8.659 ms, region growing 763.75 ms. From 400 × 300 to 4000 × 3000 the pixel count grows 100 times and the runtime 24.4 times, from 0.355 ms to 8.659 ms.

As a correctness check, with binary input and threshold 1 the method finds exactly the same number of components as OpenCV and a classical two-pass algorithm on three test images, with 475, 12,484 and 91,737 components (Table 3). The authors attribute the small differences to region growing in the IoU comparison to floating-point differences between CPU and GPU.

A stage breakdown on a 1920 × 1080 image (Table 5) shows where the time goes: initial labeling 0.608 ms, boundary detection and mapping 0.693 ms, global region-ID merging only 0.028 ms, and final relabeling with statistics 0.165 ms. The threshold τ sets how fine the segmentation is; since the runtime hardly changes with the number of components, it can be tuned without a latency penalty. Because merging is transitive, a gradual intensity ramp stays one component as long as each step between neighbouring pixels is within τ. As future work, the authors name adaptive thresholding, topology-aware boundary rules and multi-GPU extensions.

item.title: Parallel Curvature Filter for High Performance Image Processing
item.description:
The problem

The curvature filter smooths and denoises an image by implicitly reducing a curvature energy, such as Gaussian curvature, mean curvature or total variation. It treats the image as a surface and repeatedly applies a cheap local operator to every pixel, each pass lowering the regularisation energy. The filter is fast, but many images that need enhancing are high-resolution or must be processed in real or near-real time, and on a CPU a large image such as 2048 × 2048 still takes minutes.

The most expensive part of the filter is a set of eight convolutions over the image. Inspired by the way GPUs run the convolutions of convolutional neural networks, the authors parallelise these convolutions on the GPU.

How it works

Each iteration of the curvature filter enumerates eight candidate moves for every pixel, picks the smallest one and applies it. PCF computes the eight candidates for all pixels at once with convolution kernels on the GPU.

  1. The image as a surface. The image intensity U is interpreted as a surface over the pixel grid. The curvature regularisers all work on the local 3 × 3 neighbourhood around each pixel.
  2. Eight tangent-plane projections. A surface can be locally approximated by its tangent plane. In the 3 × 3 neighbourhood, eight tangent planes through neighbouring pixels are enumerated, giving eight projection distances d1 … d8 for the centre pixel.
  3. Eight convolutions on the GPU. Each distance is computed for every pixel at once as a convolution of the image. These eight convolutions are the most computationally expensive part of the algorithm; PCF runs them in CUDA and uses the GPU’s shared memory to accelerate them.
  4. Pick the smallest distance and update. For every pixel, the distance dm with the smallest magnitude is selected (ABSMIN) and added to the pixel: Ut+1 = Ut + dm. The smallest distance indicates the closest fit to the desired geometry and to the original image.
  5. Iterate. Repeating the update regularises the image surface step by step, which the paper shows by plotting the intensity along one line of the image after 10 and 30 iterations.

Results

33.2 gigapixels per second on a single GPU.
About 87 s on the CPU versus about 6 s on the GPU for 3,000 iterations on the same image (Fig. 3).

The CUDA implementation was run with GPU block sizes from 16 to 32 on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX 1080 Ti (3,584 CUDA cores, 11,264 MB of global memory, 49,152 bytes of shared memory per block) and compared with the original curvature filter on an Intel Xeon E5-1620 v4 CPU at 3.50 GHz. In Fig. 3 the computation time grows with the number of iterations on both, but far more slowly on the GPU. The authors conclude that this speed makes the filter suitable for real-time applications such as video processing and biomedical image processing.

The paper also applies Gaussian-curvature and mean-curvature versions of PCF to a photograph and plots the intensity along one line after 10 and 30 iterations. In both, the profile becomes smoother as iterations accumulate; judging from these profiles, the authors find the mean-curvature PCF more efficient at smoothing than the Gaussian-curvature PCF (a comparison of smoothing, not of running time).
